result:
There is a small café on the corner of my street that only opens between 6 and 9 am. I have never gone inside. I just like to watch it from the bus stop. The owner, a woman in her sixties with silver hair tied back, unlocks the door with the same slow ritual every morning. She wipes the windows, even though they are already clean, and arranges three chipped mugs on the counter like a small audience.

I think about how many mornings she has done this. How many times she has turned the key, how many times the bell above the door has jingled for strangers. Maybe she knows their orders by heart. Maybe she pretends not to.

Last Tuesday it rained. She forgot the umbrella and got soaked. She still wiped the windows. I felt a strange kinship with her, this woman who tends a tiny room for three hours a day. We both like routines that look pointless to everyone else.

I wonder what she does after nine. Does she close the shutters and go home? Does she sit in the dark and feel the quiet settle? I like the idea that some people make their lives out of small, repeatable acts of care.

I will probably never buy a coffee there. The thought of interrupting her ritual feels rude. So I will keep watching from the bus stop, and in my head I will order a flat white, and I will imagine she smiles and says, 'Coming right up,' to no one at all.
